claim: StackBlitz WebContainers initial payload is under one megabyte because the Node.js runtime is compiled to WebAssembly via Rust, making the in-browser runtime itself a small download even though npm install pulls happen later.
quote: WebContainers bundle size is very light, clocking in at under a megabyte... written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly to achieve this optimal size.

claim: Once the WebContainer is bootstrapped it runs offline because the Node.js runtime, package manager and a virtualized TCP stack all execute inside the browser tab.
quote: Builds complete up to 20% faster and package installs complete >= 5x faster than yarn/npm... Zero footprint. Boots in milliseconds

claim: Bolt.new's official troubleshooting guide blames most WebContainer startup failures on non-Chromium browsers, ad-blocker extensions, or VPNs interfering with the cross-origin isolation handshake — all common on locked-down conference laptops.
quote: Make sure you're using Chrome or another Chromium-based browser... Temporarily disable browser extensions, especially ad blockers... If you're using a VPN, turn it off and try again.

claim: On flaky or slow connections users routinely hit a hard 30-second boot timeout for the WebContainer, after which Bolt.new refuses to start — there is no partial-load fallback.
quote: WebContainer took longer than 30s to boot

claim: Cursor needs HTTP/2 streaming to *.cursor.sh, *.cursor-cdn.com and *.cursorapi.com; corporate or captive-portal proxies that block HTTP/2 require manually toggling an HTTP/1.1 fallback in settings before chat or agent mode works.
quote: Cursor uses HTTP/2 for streaming responses. Some corporate proxies block this protocol, so Cursor offers fallback to HTTP/1.1 compatibility mode.

claim: Cursor users report chronic streaming disconnections roughly weekly, and the recommended workaround is disabling HTTP/2 — a restart of the IDE is often needed before chat works again after a network blip.
quote: Cursor keeps disconnecting repeatedly again... Disabling HTTP/2 in settings (noted as 'most common fix')

claim: Claude Code silently hangs with a spinner instead of surfacing an error when the network drops, so on a flaky wifi a user can wait 60+ seconds before realizing the request never went through; Anthropic marked the fix request as not planned.
quote: When there's no internet connection, Claude Code silently continues with no error notification... The spinner keeps going and tool calls appear to proceed... Status: The issue was closed as 'not planned'

claim: Claude Code uses roughly 5.5x fewer tokens than Cursor on identical tasks, which translates directly into less bytes streamed over the wire per edit — a meaningful difference when 30 people share a single conference SSID.
quote: Claude Code uses 5.5x fewer tokens than Cursor on identical tasks

claim: Replit and similar fully cloud-hosted IDEs require continuous internet and lose access entirely during outages; continuous sync also burns mobile data fast when used on a tethered phone.
quote: As a cloud-based platform, Replit requires continuous internet access, which may be a challenge in areas with unstable connectivity... continuous synchronization can consume significant mobile data, and there's an inability to work during network outages

claim: Lovable apps generated after May 2026 ship as TanStack Start SSR projects, meaning the heavy rendering and AI inference happen server-side and only HTML chunks stream back to the browser — a thin-client profile that tolerates low bandwidth better than Bolt's WebContainer model.
quote: New Lovable apps created from May 13, 2026 use TanStack Start with server-side rendering (SSR)

claim: Venue wifi commonly fails at hackathons and coding workshops because 100+ laptops simultaneously pulling npm, pushing to GitHub and streaming previews saturate APs not provisioned for power users; backup hotspot kits are now standard recommendation.
quote: Venue WiFi often buckles under hackathon traffic, where participants push commits to GitHub, live-stream demos, and pull API data—heavy-duty, all-at-once usage by power users. When 200 laptops all submit projects simultaneously, a weak network can derail the experience.

claim: GitHub Codespaces (and remote IDEs that follow the same model) preserve running processes and saved files across disconnects — you can drop wifi, walk to the back of the room, and resume the same shell session, which Bolt.new in-tab WebContainers cannot do once the tab closes.
quote: You can disconnect and reconnect to an active codespace without affecting its running processes. Any saved changes in your codespace will still be available when you next start it.
